articles.title_orig: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title_orig: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.title_zh: European Union and UK strike a 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.
Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."
Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."
He went further and said " Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
The three key agreements establish ways to:
The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.
No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.
Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."
On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.
According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.
Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.
The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit .
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

articles.title_orig: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.title_zh: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.content_orig:
Two new reports on the housing market show activity slowing even more, after a September spike in mortgage rates sent it into a deep freeze.
Pending home sales in October dropped 4.7% month-over-month and were down 16.7% from October of last year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This is the lowest level in the index's 25-year history.
Analysts had been looking for a much smaller decline, likely because mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, only to rise sharply again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed started October at 7.54% according to Mortgage News Daily and ended the month at 7.27%.
The pending count is based on signed contracts — people out shopping and signing deals during the month. It is therefore an indicator of future closed sales.
"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.
Regionally, sales were down across the nation with the sharpest drops in the South, which is usually busiest for sales and the West which is most expensive.
Another report released Wednesday showed gains in home construction in October but raised a red flag going forward. Single-family housing starts rose 4% from September, according to the U.S. Census, but were down 3.2% year over year. Building permits, an indicator of future construction, dropped 8.7% for the month and were down 12.9% from October 2025. That is the lowest level for permits since May 2020, the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it's rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," wrote Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "This month's data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."
The construction report follows a bleak reading on homebuilder sentiment , which fell to the lowest level in 14 years in November, on the monthly index from the National Association of Home Builders. Builders cited multiple challenges, including higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.title_zh: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Drops Below $150 Support After Jensen Huang Scandal: Key Levels to Watch
articles.content_orig:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares fell 12% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang . The stock is poised to close lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 44% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by $2.5 trillion. The stock is now trading at around 9.3 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company, now, at a market cap of $3.1 trillion, Nvidia is fourth behind Apple and Microsoft and Alphabet .
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the  AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
How much is a CEO worth? As I am writing this column, the Nvidia share price has fallen by more than 12 percent since the allegations of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, followed by other allegations of affairs with women who work at Nvidia, and Huang’s subsequent exit from the company. That represents a value loss of about $570 billion, bringing the market capitalization of the company under $4 trillion. If we go back to October 6, the company has fallen in value by more than 30 percent since that date, or about $1.85 trillion. It’s no surprise that, despite everything, the Financial Times reported Sunday that Huang is considering a comeback, backed by his allies in Silicon Valley.
We’ll have a better sense of Huang’s overall value to his company once more facts are in. If his indiscretions drag down the company in the long run, along with the sudden leadership change, that will count against him. And if he schemed to evade U.S. export controls, that would partly overshadow his contributions because of the importance of national security.
But from a purely material standpoint, Huang excelled in co-founding Nvidia, driving its growth aggressively, and seeing how important it was to cultivate the AI sector as a whole to boost the demand for the company’s GPUs and other products.
Huang is an extreme example of a truth I believe is borne out by the evidence: that despite the fulminating about executive pay, many top CEOs are in fact significantly underpaid. As a first-order approximation, one might say he was worth at least $570 billion to Nvidia, far more than he was paid. His net worth previously was estimated at about $200 billion , now probably more in the range of $140 billion , and that likely comprises most of his lifetime earnings in the form of Nvidia stock. Furthermore, the Nvidia crisis has driven down share prices across the AI industry. You could attribute some of that loss to Huang’s departure, which means he was even more underpaid from an economy-wide perspective.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.title_zh: Iraqi Forces Enter Stronghold of Powerful Iran-Backed Militia
articles.content_orig:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says his country’s security forces will establish a joint operations centre in the town of Jurf al-Sakhar, in a compromise with the Iranian-backed Kataib Hezbollah armed group over control of a strategic area south of Baghdad.
The Jurf al-Sakhar area has long been a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah, and the new agreement comes after the Iraqi government announced plans to send in security forces amid allegations that the group was smuggling oil.
The compromise reached late on Thursday will see a new combined force deployed to the area, consisting of a brigade from the Iraqi army, a brigade from the Federal Police, a regiment from the Energy Police to provide protection for oil pipelines in the area, and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are officially part of Iraq’s security forces, including some Kataib Hezbollah fighters.
A military spokesman said the new joint operations centre will open at 6am local time (03:00 GMT) on Friday morning.
In a statement, the PMF said their forces will begin replacing the military units stationed in Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, in accordance with the directives from Prime Minister al-Zaidi.
Earlier in the week, an Iraqi official told Al Jazeera that the commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, arrived in Iraq to push for a solution due to the simmering tensions with Iran.
A Kataib Hezbollah spokesman confirmed that Qaani met with senior members of their organisation, as well as the head of PMF and a representative from the Badr Organization, an Iranian-backed political group that also contributes armed fighters to the PMF.
In a statement, Kataib Hezbollah said the talks addressed the current crisis and described the outcomes of the discussions as positive.
Separately, in a news conference on Thursday, Kataib Hezbollah expressed appreciation for the PMF and Iraqi security forces for preventing escalating tensions that serve “the enemies”. The group also affirmed that any existing issues would be resolved through private channels.
A senior Iraqi official previously told Al Jazeera that Kataib Hezbollah had until Friday to leave Jurf al-Sakhar. The group had threatened to confront government troops and had rejected the government’s efforts to disarm non-state militias.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoy Jared Kushner has said Russia may accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, adding that President Donald Trump wants to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion "with Europe by his side."
His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.
"I think we've got the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5," Kushner said alongside European leaders at a news conference in Germany on Thursday, referring to the part of NATO's treaty that enshrines the principle of collective defense.
"I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is, when this war is over, to not have another war in the future," he added. Kushner, who is Trump's son-in-law, was at the conference in Berlin alongside fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
They have led the Trump administration's efforts to end Russia's nearly five-year-long war with Ukraine.
Article 5 defines an attack against one NATO member as an attack against all members. The alliance calls it a "unique and enduring principle that binds its members together, committing them to protect each other and setting a spirit of solidarity."
Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance. Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.
It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, or whether Russia or Ukraine would accept them. Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.
"From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal and I think that that is something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that," Kushner said.
Russia launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's energy and transport infrastructure overnight, damaging three bridges in Kyiv and killing at least three people, authorities said.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said via Telegram on Friday that Kyiv's Podilskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern crossings had been damaged by missile strikes, with experts currently assessing the damage.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had carried out a "massive" strike on several Ukrainian cities, targeting enterprises of the country's defense industry and warehouses used in the production and storage of missiles and drones.
Putin vowed on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge , adding it would be "much more painful." The bridge, which links Russia to occupied Crimea and is one of Putin's signature projects, was damaged by repeated Ukrainian attacks this week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday described it as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

articles.title_orig: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.title_zh: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.content_orig:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

articles.title_orig: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.title_zh: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has agreed a “reset” deal with Brussels , calling it “a good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”.
The Prime Minister hailed deals on food, youth mobility and carbon emissions, but talks on how much EU students should be charged for studying at UK universities stalled.
What exactly has been agreed, and what does it mean for the UK and the EU ?
The Youth Experience Scheme is the centrepiece of the reset deal.
It will allow 100,000 young Europeans, aged 18 to 31, to live, work and study in Britain for up to three years, and for Britons to do the same across the EU member states.
The final figure agreed is much higher than the original UK proposal of a cap of 30,000 to 50,000 young people .
It will raise concerns that the number could undermine the Government’s plans to reduce the number of Britons under 25 on welfare and not in education, employment or training (Neets).
With almost one million Neets in the UK , ministers have signed up to Alan Milburn’s reforms to reduce the rate from the current 15 per cent of young people to 5 per cent.
The joint statement, signed by the UK and EU, states that both sides will endeavour to open up the scheme no later than January 2030. This means the full effect on UK migration figures will not be available until after the next election, which must be held no later than 2029.
However, the two sides failed to clinch a deal on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain.
The EU wants its students to pay the same domestic fees as British counterparts, rather than the higher overseas charge, but UK negotiators have resisted this.
Instead, the two sides agreed to revisit the issue later and reach an agreement in six months. But in a meeting late on Thursday night, EU capitals warned that they would not implement the reset deals until the tuition fees dispute is resolved.
Britain has agreed to align with EU rules on plant and animal health to boost trade and try to lessen the cost of living crisis.
The Government says the agreement will make imports and exports cheaper and, as a consequence, the weekly shop will become less expensive. It is also expected to add up to £5.1bn a year for the UK economy.
It will ease trade between Britain and Northern Ireland over the post-Brexit Irish Sea border . The deal also means the return of EU pet passports for British tourists wanting to take their dogs, cats and ferrets on holiday.
But it comes at a cost to British sovereignty. The UK has become an EU rule-taker , changing its laws to match those of Brussels without having any real say in their drafting.
London will point to language in the agreement, which discusses Britain having a role in “shaping” decisions on regulation. However, this is a fig leaf.
The European Commission jealously guards its power to legislate and the concerns of a 60 million-strong UK market are dwarfed by the size of the single market’s 460 million consumers.
The EU already allows other non-EU members of the single market – such as Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein – to have a non-binding say on incoming legislation, but in practice it makes little difference.
Both sides want the agreement to apply from 2028.
The UK will rejoin the EU’s Emissions Trading System, a carbon market that aims to accelerate the push to net zero by cutting pollution.
A major benefit of this for Britain is that it will spare the UK from falling foul of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
CBAM is a tariff wall designed to shield EU businesses from competition from other countries exporting cheaper goods made to lower environmental standards.
Being part of the EU’s carbon market will strengthen British arguments that it should not be hit by the higher tariffs aimed principally at countries like China.
But again it involves alignment with EU rules and accepting that the European Court of Justice will be the final arbiter of those rules. That will be a bitter pill for Brexiteers to swallow, as they campaigned for an end to decisions being made in foreign courts holding sway in Britain.
The aim is to ensure the UK joins the world’s largest carbon market in 2028.
Mr Burnham wanted assurances the EU’s new Made in Europe Act would not hurt British industries.
Instead, UK negotiators were only able to secure vague language about the need to protect each other’s supply chains.
The act is designed to favour EU companies against cheaper Chinese imports through subsidies.
Britain fears its car industry, green technologies, and steel and aluminium sectors would have been affected if they were shut out of European subsidies.
The Made In Europe Act is still under negotiation in the EU. It is expected to be finalised in six months, allowing talks over Britain’s involvement to be tied to the tuition fees discussions.
Many in Brussels believe the Brexit reset was only possible because of the fragile geopolitical context, and the joint statement makes that clear.
It declares joint support for Ukraine as well as their opposition to Russia and the war in Iran.
What is also interesting is that it makes a direct reference to the EU’s and UK’s backing for the UN and International Criminal Court – a thinly-veiled swipe at Donald Trump’s attacks on the institutions.
There is little in the way of concrete outcomes from the latest reset deal other than a path for Britain to contribute to the EU’s civilian missions under its Common Security and Defence Policy.
This means non-military officials could be deployed alongside EU counterparts on missions designed to uphold peace and democracy outside Europe.
The UK and EU also called for respect for international law in Gaza and condemned settler violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank.
The UK and EU have formalised their discussions on illegal migration into a so-called “structured dialogue on migration”.
It doesn’t mean a great deal at this moment, but Mr Burnham hopes it will pave the way for genuine cooperation to fight small boat crossings .
Discussions are set to make up the bulk of future negotiations before next year’s set piece EU-UK summit.
The language agreed in the joint statement suggests the first efforts will focus on reinstating data-sharing agreements that ended after Brexit, such as over criminal and asylum databases.
It also opens the door to Britain joining a Rwanda-like plan devised by five EU states to send failed asylum seekers to the East African country.
Britain has agreed to make contributions to EU funding for poorer European regions in return for access to the EU’s electricity market.
There will be further negotiations on how this will work and how much it will cost.

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.title_zh: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.content_orig:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.
The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.
Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.
His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.
Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.
He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.
The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.
He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.
It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".
Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".
He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".
After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.
Joel Smith KC, prosecuting, said it was "more a matter of luck than judgement that serious consequences did not arise".
The dinghy was later destroyed by French authorities, meaning the value of the damage could not be proven.
Judge James Newton-Price KC said it was "not for me to make any judgement of the political cause," but that the attack was "intended to have an impact on a live audience".
Commenting on the Border Force, coastguard and RNLI crews, he said: "They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover."
Simon Pentol KC, defending, said the dinghy did not sink and made its way back to France without help.
The judge accepted that prison had caused hardship for Thomas's family, including his four children. He said the sentence would have been 20 months had he gone to trial, and his time on remand would count towards it.
A separate charge of failing to give police the PIN to his phone, which Thomas denied, was ordered to lie on his file.
He is due to stand trial at Westminster Magistrates' Court in June over separate alleged offences in Dover, which he denies.

articles.title_orig: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.title_zh: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.content_orig:
12th Joint Committee Meeting reviews progress and explores new opportunities to strengthen cooperation on employment, skills, social protection and emerging challenges in the world of work.
GENEVA (ILO News) – The International Labour Organization (ILO) and China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) have reaffirmed their commitment to advancing decent work and social justice through South-South cooperation, with a focus on emerging labour-market challenges and partnerships across the Global South.
The commitment was highlighted at the 12th Joint Committee Meeting on ILO–China Cooperation, held in Geneva on 20 November 2026. The meeting reviewed progress since the previous Joint Committee Meeting in 2021 and explored opportunities to deepen cooperation.
The discussions took place against a backdrop of rapid technological change, persistent labour-market inequalities and the need to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
Participants underscored the importance of translating development cooperation into practical improvements focusing on areas of longstanding cooperation including employment opportunities, skills and social protection.
Since 2021, China-supported ILO initiatives have contributed to strengthening institutional capacity, policy exchange and knowledge sharing, particularly across countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
Cooperation in skills development has supported training institutions and responses to growing demand for digital, green and industry-relevant skills. Employment initiatives have promoted high-quality and full employment, stronger public employment services, entrepreneurship and regional policy dialogue. In social protection, cooperation has supported efforts to expand coverage and improve service delivery, including through digital transformation.
Participants emphasized the importance of building on these achievements, sharing good practices and strengthening national institutions to ensure sustainable results.
Looking ahead, discussions explored how South-South cooperation could help countries navigate changes in the world of work, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence and the platform economy.
Participants considered opportunities to harness technological innovation for productivity and employment while addressing potential risks for workers and enterprises. They also highlighted the importance of connecting country-level initiatives with regional and global policy dialogue to broaden the impact of development cooperation.
The meeting further considered the role of the ILO–China partnership within wider development frameworks including the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). China’s presidency of the BRICs in 2027 will also offer an important opportunity to advance cooperation on various world of work issues.
China has been a member of the ILO since its founding and has developed a longstanding partnership with the Organization. The ILO–China cooperation framework encompasses employment promotion, skills development, social protection, occupational safety and health, and South-South cooperation. Through technical cooperation, policy dialogue and knowledge exchange, the partnership supports countries in advancing decent work and meeting the Sustainable Development Goals.

China’s crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf surged by 42.4% in October from September, to the highest level since the Iran war began, as supply via the Strait of Hormuz rebounded and Gulf producers slashed prices for their crude to attract buyers amid record-high freight rates.
China imported 19.7 million tons of crude oil from the Persian Gulf producers, excluding Iran, in October, a 42.4% jump from the previous month, per calculations by the South China Morning Post based on Chinese customs data released on Friday.
October was the fourth consecutive month in which Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf countries increased from the previous month, according to the data.
Gulf producers shipped almost half of total Chinese term supplies last month, at a level approaching the pre-war volumes, the estimates by the South China Morning Post showed.
The surge in Chinese imports from the Gulf coincided with the recovery of crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Additionally, Gulf producers reduced the prices of their crude grades loading for Asia as Hormuz flows rebounded and pressured down Middle Eastern crude benchmarks.
Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recovered and reached pre-war levels on some days.
Lower prices for December are expected to continue attracting buying interest in China, especially amid the slide in international crude oil prices.
Saudi oil giant Aramco earlier this month slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount for Saudi crude to the Middle East’s benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic.

articles.title_orig: Ex-Super Micro exec married to Nvidia’s former sales chief says she took CEO job days before smuggling scandal broke
articles.title_zh: Ex-Super Micro exec married to Nvidia’s former sales chief says she took CEO job days before smuggling scandal broke
articles.content_orig:
Published: 08:28 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 10:33 EST, 20 November 2026
A grammar school pupil took her own life two days after her parents' wedding, a court heard.
Mikelle Hardy-Ingham, 16, died at home in June 2024 after taking an overdose of medication prescribed to a family member.
An inquest at Devon Coroner's Court heard that Mikelle had run away a couple of days earlier after a row with her mother Tina.
However, her aunt Lesley Taylor picked her up from the station and the family appeared to reconcile.
But on the morning of June 16 one of her siblings, whose room Mikelle was sleeping in, told their father, Lee, that she had blood around her mouth.
When Mr Hardy-Ingham saw his daughter, there was dried blood on her mouth and her body was cold.
He called 999, and an ambulance arrived at the scene in Torquay, Devon, but Mikelle was pronounced dead at her home.
Mikelle Hardy-Ingham was a talented poet, songwriter and radio DJ who dreamed of becoming a journalist
Mikelle's family described her as funny, caring and loyal, with a passion for writing, music and helping others
Mikelle's mum, Tina (pictured), wants her daughter to be remembered for the positive impact she hoped to have on other young people
The court heard that Mikelle, who had attempted to take her own life in 2021, had been appointed as a mental health ambassador at Torquay Girls' Grammar School, where she was a student.
Mr Hardy-Ingham, a father of four, said Mikelle had her own show on local radio station Palm FM and had plans to attend sixth form and then go to university in London to become a journalist.
He added: 'She was passionate about people being able to talk about their mental health.'
Mikelle had seen mental health professionals and was taking the antidepressant sertraline, having been diagnosed with depression, anxiety and an Autistic Spectrum Disorder.
Not long before her death, a fellow student had 'latched on to' her in her role as mental health ambassador and had started following her around.
That meant she had taken her exams in isolation and made her feel like she was being punished and not able to see her friends.
In May 2024, she was the victim of an assault, the court heard. When she reported the incident to the police, she started getting threatening messages on her phone and on her social media.
Mikelle's parents got married on June 13, but when her mother returned from her honeymoon briefly to check on Mikelle, she found that she was with a couple of people whom Tina did not know.
When she tried to get the teenagers out of the house, they initially refused and when they did leave, there was an argument between mother and daughter, which led to Mikelle running off.
She was found by police and her aunt picked her up. Her father returned from the holiday, and her mother went off to stay at a family member's caravan.
The court heard that, after Mikelle's 2021 overdose, her father had taken to locking his medication in a safe, which he kept on top of the wardrobe in the bedroom he shared with his partner.
But when police examined the scene of Mikelle's death, they found a notebook with a suicide note and a key to Mr Hardy-Ingham's medicine safe.
A toxicology report found that Mikelle had more than three times the fatal amount of a prescription drug in her bloodstream.
Making a finding of suicide, Coroner Alison Longhorn said: 'Mikelle was a truly exceptional young lady.
'I offer my condolences to you. I can't imagine what it must be like.'
Mikelle was a published poet, songwriter for local band Falling Off A Horse, and a passionate writer who loved exploring big philosophical questions.
Just weeks before her death, she presented a bid to the local council for a £400 bursary to create a magazine supporting young people's mental health, with proceeds intended for Mind.

articles.title_orig: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.title_zh: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.content_orig:
Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough."
He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.
Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."
Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."
His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.
Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.
"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.
The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.
Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.
Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.
A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.
GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.
That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."
When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.
Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.
Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.
"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."
Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.
Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.
"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday.
Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country.
Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed.
The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers.
What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement .
Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so.
The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands.
By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter.

articles.title_orig: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.title_zh: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck a deal on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang spent 30 years building Nvidia, quit when his indiscretions were revealed , then days later issued a plea to return as CEO.
The company’s stock slumped, not just amid controversy over whether some of its chips ended up in China, where they were banned, but by a far greater amount when Huang left .
And given Nvidia is known as the “Central Bank of AI,” other industry darlings like CoreWeave and Nebius have fallen even harder.
As Nvidia gets hit, it’s not just millions of Americans seeing their 401(k)s drop precipitously, but the entire fragile AI ecosystem Nvidia has spent billions building could be in jeopardy.
Many of the most powerful figures in tech have since rallied behind a “save Jensen Huang” campaign, fearing Nvidia may be a beast with its head cut off without him.
Bigwigs such as Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator chief Garry Tan and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke are among more than 250,000 people who have signed a letter asking for due process and a fair hearing, rather than blindly reinstating the legendary chip boss.
Memes going viral online — many generated using the very chips Huang’s company built —cast Huang as the rightful king returning to the throne (although, to be fair, far more of them are ridiculing him).
It’s not unheard of. In fact, Huang would join many founders who were ousted and ultimately returned to the companies they built.
Sam Altman was fired from OpenAI but returned just five days later. Jack Dorsey (Twitter), Steve Jobs (Apple), and Howard Schultz (Starbucks) each spent years away from the companies they built before being reinstated.
However, to be fair, none of those people were kicked out for allegedly sleeping with spies.
Huang quit after revelations of his closeness to Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative he had been selling chips to, which may have ended up in China.
Further allegations of him sleeping with two subordinates at Nvidia are immoral, unethical and against company standards — and, detractors are quick to say, disqualifying.
But sometimes someone is so singular that, for the good of a nation, flaws that can be overlooked should be overlooked. That is exactly how people in the chip industry see Huang — a unique builder and visionary who spent three decades creating a company that only he can run and that has become critical for the American winning the AI revolution.
Until quite recently, Huang secured critical links in America’s chip supply chain with handshakes and relationships only he could develop. The fact an American leader was admired by Chinese engineers and seen as the pre-eminent voice gave him a unique kind of diplomacy in the region.
Losing that influence is a blow to our dominance and security — and risks giving our foreign adversaries a major advantage.
Palmer Luckey recently made the argument that China’s desire to see Huang, born in Taiwan, out should be enough to raise alarm bells — and strengthen the case for bringing him back.
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” he posted earlier this week. Given, that his ouster benefits China, shouldn’t we proceed with caution?
What if we’d sidelined Robert Oppenheimer during the Manhattan Project, or Henry Ford as he built out the American auto industry?
Amid a new race for geopolitical dominance, do we really want to sic the morality police on one of the greatest men of our times without weighing the consequences? In an age when orgies, drugs and various much worse debauchery is the norm in Silicon Valley, are we going to handicap ourselves to prove a point?
Huang’s stance was somewhat controversial, that American needs to sell chips to China’s huge market of 1.3 billion people — a view hated by many hawks. He believed the goal should be to keep China buying from us, rather than cut it off entirely.
We still don’t know what Jensen knew and when he knew it, or whether he could be implicated in the billions of dollars’ worth of chips his alleged mistress’s company, Megaspeed, is accused of diverting to China in violation of US export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has suspicions questioning whether Nvidia executives were “pressing seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings,” or using shell companies “as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese.”
But Silicon Valley—which is not exactly filled with prudes —is already onto the next question: why, after months of this relationship allegedly going on, is it only emerging now, and who stands to benefit?
So far, the only clear wrongdoing is the leak of a classified memo to the New York Times. That memo, drafted under Secretary of State Marco Rubio, warned of Huang’s relationship with a possible Chinese asset. It also revealed some officials were concerned about Huang’s growing influence over Trump’s AI policy.
Huang had become powerful enough in he effectively supplanted the authority of important figures in Washington — so sidelining him gives officials more control.
The timing is also striking: the story broke just before Anthropic’s IPO.  And Nvidia has allegedly been developing an open source AI model which could rival Anthropic’s. Removing Huang weakens a potential competitor, while leaving Anthropic in a stronger position.
Huang also resigned quickly — just days after the scandal broke — rather than standing his ground and waiting for a full investigation, which doesn’t help his comeback cause.
DOJ chief Todd Blanche’s recent comments that actually Alice Huang may not be a spy raises the question of whether the story that prompted Jensen to step down even matters anymore.
Huang’s post saying he’d be “honored to return” has garnered upwards of a million likes.
We’ll find out more when he testifies in front of Congress next week. But he should also fight, the future of American AI supremacy could be on the line.

articles.title_orig: The Best Early-Game ‘GTA 6’ Vehicle Isn’t Hidden Or Expensive
articles.title_zh: The Best Early-Game ‘GTA 6’ Vehicle Isn’t Hidden Or Expensive
articles.content_orig:
Join 100K+ fans and never miss breaking news, fan theories, trailers and exclusive content.
Grand Theft Auto 6 ( GTA 6 ) is what everyone’s playing right now, and one detail that we’re noticing is that the story starts off pretty slow. Once you complete Chapter 1, the game finally puts you in the shoes of Lucia as you try to recover your situation in Port Gellhorn. Early into the story, you’ll unlock Moses Watkins’ garage in Port Gellhorn, and you’ll finally be able to register a personal vehicle.
GTA 6 Prepare for Vice City: How to Earn the $15,000 Fast

Stolen cars for Moses are the steadiest money, about $1,000 or more each.

#GTA6

@RockstarGames https://t.co/t2YWHlHHNw
You can only register vehicles without anti-theft GPS trackers at Moses’ workshop, and your first registration with him is completely free, so you’ll want to find the best vehicle to register. Once you register a vehicle, you can summon it anytime through the Scooter Bros app. Very cool mechanic, Rockstar Games .
The Emperor Sultan is one of the easiest cars to find in Port Gellhorn. This four-door sedan is a good overall car for all activities you’ll encounter in Chapter 2. And even if you don’t find one, you can earn Moses’ personal Emperor Sultan directly by completing his Port Gellhorn vehicle drop-off requests, registering it for just $1,600. It has good cornering, four-seat capacity, and generous trunk space, making it great for storing weapons, outfits, and any items you find.
In fourth place is the Dinka Chavos XS. It has a 497 road rating, 5.2 top speed, and 5.7 acceleration. The handling is great on both roads and light dirt paths. While it lacks the sheer muscle of the Dominator or Phoenix, it has a low-profile look, solid trunk storage, and can be found in the nearby area south of Port Gellhorn called Capri.
While not technically a car, the Nagasaki SFB 1000 is the best getaway vehicle you can register in Chapter 2. You can also find this in the nearby posh area of Capri. This sport motorcycle will get you through thick traffic and in tight spaces where cars just don’t fit. Just remember that riding two wheels trades away trunk storage and collision protection, making it the best for solo recon and quick escapes.
If you want classic GTA style paired with heavy V8 punch, the Imponte ’77 Phoenix is the car for you. The best part about it is that you can find it in Port Gellhorn itself, just south of the La Cascara Motel. With rear-wheel-drive muscle tuning, this retro coupe will zoom down highways and has plenty of visual customization options at local mod shops. Its vintage build keeps it free of modern anti-theft trackers, making it a great pick for your free initial registration.
Taking the top spot for best performance and style, the Vapid Firebug Dominator is a great modern muscle vehicle. You’ll easily outrun standard patrol cruisers and anything else Chapter 2 throws at you. It is a guaranteed spawn at the La Cascara Motel in Port Gellhorn, and you can bring it to Moses for a quick respray.
Before driving any boosted vehicle in Port Gellhorn, pull out Lucia’s phone and scan it with the WAiNK app to verify that the security readout shows no tracker installed. Use the Slim Jim Moses provides to slip past door locks quietly without triggering alarms or drawing unwanted police heat.
Keep in mind that Moses will reject vehicles stolen right outside his shop, so grab your target a few blocks down the road. Once inside his bay, you’ll have to apply a fresh respray before the registration option unlocks. And make sure you have an open garage slot ready if you plan to expand beyond your first free claim.
Which of these vehicles did you register for Lucia in GTA 6 Chapter 2? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.
Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.
It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington . The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.
But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.
The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.
SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.
Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."
"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training.
The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.
Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely , via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using " distillation ," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
